The brief

A demo that runs the whole process, not a scripted walkthrough

The goal was an agent that waits for an inbound message, then works a lead all the way to a booked appointment on its own: greeting, qualification, package fit, time zone, live slot offer, contact capture, booking. No canned responses, no human in the loop.

The agent runs on a Hostinger VPS inside a Hermes container. Its persona, pricing, hours and booking rules come from five markdown documents describing a fictional Tampa marketing agency, Harbor & Pine. The setter is Ava, their Client Care Coordinator.

Audit

What the starting point actually was

The brief said the agent was already connected to GoHighLevel and Supabase. A read-only audit of the VPS, the container, both APIs and the agent's own message history found something different.

01

The integrations were never saved

The "connection" was a one-off curl test inside a terminal tool call. Nothing was written to the agent's config or environment, so the credentials existed only in chat history. A fresh session knew nothing about either service.

02

The CRM token could not book

Probing the GoHighLevel token endpoint by endpoint showed it held contacts, conversations, calendars and locations, but returned 401 on calendars/events, opportunities, customFields, tags and users. The one scope that creates appointments was missing.

03

The database was empty

Supabase held the five knowledge documents in a storage bucket and nothing else. Zero tables. There was nowhere to write a lead, a message or a booking.

04

Nothing could reach the agent

Inbound webhooks need HTTPS. The compose file carried Traefik labels but no Traefik container existed, so port 443 was closed. The only public surface was the agent dashboard on plain HTTP over port 32768.

05

A previous bot was still live

The sub-account carried four published workflows from an earlier booking bot. Left running, every lead would have received two replies.

Decision

Rather than repair five problems inside someone else's CRM, the CRM itself became the thing to build. That removed the token scopes, the webhook requirement, the workflow conflict and the third-party dependency in one move, and made every rule in the source documents directly enforceable.

Architecture

Three services, one box, outbound only

The agent never accepts an inbound connection. It polls the API over the internal Docker network, which removed the reverse-proxy requirement that blocked the original design and kept the container unexposed.

Message flow

What happens between send and reply

  1. The message lands. A row is written to messages as inbound and unhandled; a lead, conversation and opportunity are created on the first one.
  2. The worker picks it up within a second and requests context: the lead record, conversation history, open slots per calendar.
  3. Knowledge is retrieved. The message is embedded and matched against the document chunks by vector similarity, fused with Postgres full-text ranking so exact strings like a price are not missed.
  4. Ava decides. One model call returns a single JSON object: the reply, field updates, tags, pipeline stage, and a slot id when she is ready to book.
  5. The decision is applied inside the database, then broadcast over the WebSocket. The reply, the contact fields, the tags, the stage and the booking all appear at once.
Why it is split this way

Ava makes every judgement; the worker performs the writes. Letting a model drive eight CRM tools mid-conversation is where live demos fail. Keeping the decision in the model and the mutations deterministic made booking reliable without making the agent less capable.

Interface

Lead on the left, CRM on the right

You type as the lead. The record, tags, pipeline and calendar update live beside the thread, which is what makes the agent's work visible rather than implied.

Engineering notes

Three decisions worth the detail

Booking is correct by construction

Four calendars, each with its own host, duration, buffer, weekdays, minimum notice and booking window, plus office closures and a reduced holiday week.

Rather than ask the model to respect those rules, a Postgres function materialises every legal slot in advance and booking flips one to taken. Double-booking is not a rule the agent can forget; it is a unique constraint. Offering a slot inside the notice window is impossible because such a slot is never returned.

Retrieval is semantic, with a literal safety net

The five documents are chunked by section and embedded with a 384-dimension ONNX model running on the same box.

Pure vector search is weak on exact tokens, and a lead asking whether it is really $2,997 is matching a string, not a concept. Vector results are fused with Postgres full-text ranking so both kinds of question land on the right section. The embedding model was chosen for footprint: the obvious library would have pulled roughly two gigabytes of PyTorch onto a box already running the agent.

Replies got 2.6× faster after measuring where the time went

The first working version answered in about nine seconds. Profiling each layer showed the cost was not the model.

Spawning the agent CLI cost 2.8 seconds before any inference. Worse, the full agent loop expanded a 1,700-token prompt into 30,000 to 47,000 tokens by re-reasoning over a large system prompt across several internal turns, and ran anywhere from 7 to 33 seconds. Setting a lead is a single structured decision with no tool use, so the worker now calls the model directly with the same persona files as its system prompt.

Ava's behaviour still comes entirely from the same SOUL.md and skill file, so editing those changes her either way, and the slower path remains as an automatic fallback.

Result

End to end, unattended

A cold Instagram DM reaches a booked consultation without intervention. In the run captured above, the agent extracted twelve fields across the conversation, applied the correct package and booking tags, moved the opportunity through four pipeline stages, confirmed the lead's time zone before offering times, and booked a real slot on the Growth calendar with the right host.

Hardening came with the build: the agent dashboard moved off plaintext onto TLS, its published port was closed, and the firewall was switched on.

Harbor & Pine is a fictional agency built for this project. Every lead, conversation, booking and figure shown here is mock data.
